Tracts and Handbills of the Religious Tract Society is a trade list of cheap tracts. It bears the date March first, eighteen hundred forty three. William Jones sold the works at the Depository in Paternoster Row. Nisbet and Company shared the London sale of the lists.

No works save the Society’s own could be had at that house, it states. Gifts and dues went whole, with no charge cut, to free spread of tracts. Samuel Hoare kept the purse as treasurer of the whole work. First Series tracts lead the list, priced singly and by the hundred. Watts’s Songs for Children and hymns stand high in that roll. Death of Lord Rochester and Life of Colonel Gardiner draw the eye. Tracts to prisoners, servants, youths, and the fallen fill the ranks. Welsh and foreign lists were printed apart for their own crowds.

Former CBS war reporter Cookie Hood tells Danny Jones her life story. Hood covered war in Nicaragua during the 1980s. Before that she modeled in New York and married a cartel figure.

Her new show traces that wild path in her own voice. She promises the real story behind Iran-Contra, the arms and drugs scandal. She saw the war, the rebels, and the trade up close. Jones lets her connect those worlds step by step. The episode offers a rare firsthand bridge between newsrooms, cartels, and a secret war. Few reporters can match her mix of access and risk.
